claim: Altered insulin signaling has been linked to widespread nervous system dysfunction including cognitive dysfunction, neuropathy and susceptibility to neurodegenerative disease.
source: Altered insulin signaling has been linked to widespread nervous system dysfunction including cognitive dysfunction, neuropathy and susceptibility to neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these associations.

claim: Cell autonomous insulin signaling within the Drosophila CM9 motor neuron regulates the release of neurotransmitter via alteration of the synaptic vesicle fusion machinery.
source: Here, we show that cell autonomous insulin signaling within the Drosophila CM9 motor neuron regulates the release of neurotransmitter via alteration of the synaptic vesicle fusion machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including electrophysiological recordings and genetic manipulations.

claim: The effect of insulin on neurotransmitter release utilizes the FOXO-dependent regulation of the thor gene, which encodes the Drosophila homologue of the eif-4e binding protein (4eBP).
source: This effect of insulin utilizes the FOXO-dependent regulation of the thor gene, which encodes the Drosophila homologue of the eif-4e binding protein (4eBP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including genetic manipulations of FOXO and 4eBP, and molecular analyses showing FOXO binding to the 4eBP promoter.

claim: Complexin is a critical target of the insulin-4eBP regulatory mechanism.
source: A critical target of this regulatory mechanism is Complexin, a synaptic protein known to regulate synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Complexin mRNA binds to Staufen, Complexin protein levels at synapses are diet-sensitive, and genetic manipulations of Complexin affect neurotransmission.

claim: The amounts of Complexin protein observed at the synapse is regulated by insulin.
source: We find that the amounts of Complexin protein observed at the synapse is regulated by insulin and genetic manipulations of Complexin levels support the model that increased synaptic Complexin reduces neurotransmission in response to insulin signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased Complexin at synapses in 2X diet conditions and reduced Complexin in chico RNAi animals.

claim: Increased synaptic Complexin reduces neurotransmission in response to insulin signaling.
source: We find that the amounts of Complexin protein observed at the synapse is regulated by insulin and genetic manipulations of Complexin levels support the model that increased synaptic Complexin reduces neurotransmission in response to insulin signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic manipulations showing that Complexin overexpression reduces neurotransmission and Complexin reduction increases neurotransmission.

claim: Analysis of human patients with type II diabetes (T2DM) reveals changes in brain structures, including synapse numbers, which correlate with decreased cognitive performance.
source: For example, analysis of human patients with type II diabetes (T2DM) reveals changes in brain structures, including synapse numbers, which correlate with decreased cognitive performance (Qiu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Numerous rodent studies have demonstrated that changes in peripheral and cerebral insulin result in changes to synapse function and plasticity in both the hippocampus and retinae.
source: In addition, numerous rodent studies have demonstrated that changes in peripheral and cerebral insulin result in changes to synapse function and plasticity in both the hippocampus and retinae (Gispen and Biessels, 2000; Hombrebueno et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rodent and human studies have demonstrated that changes in normal insulin signaling can alter peripheral synapses including neuromuscular junctions (NMJs).
source: Rodent and human studies have also demonstrated that changes in normal insulin signaling can alter peripheral synapses including neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) (Allen et al., 2015a, 2015b; Fahim et al., 1998; Francis et al., 2011; Garcia et al., 2012; Ramji et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cellular mechanisms underlying the effects insulin signaling on synapse function, especially the control of neurotransmitter release, are poorly understood.
source: Despite the wide-spread effects of altered insulin signaling on synapse function, the cellular mechanisms underlying the effects insulin signaling on synapse function, especially the control of neurotransmitter release, are poorly understood.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on review of existing literature.

claim: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex is positively regulated by insulin signaling.
source: This includes the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex that is positively regulated by insulin signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about insulin signaling pathways.

claim: In the postsynaptic compartment, TOR signaling has been directly implicated in the regulation of post-synaptic function including the formation of new synapses and the generation of retrograde signaling during homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
source: In the postsynaptic compartment, TOR signaling has been directly implicated in the regulation of post-synaptic function including the formation of new synapses and the generation of retrograde signaling during homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Penney et al., 2012; Stoica et al., 2011; Takei and Nawa, 2014; Weston et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The role of TOR signaling within the presynaptic nerve terminal is less clear.
source: The role of TOR signaling within the presynaptic nerve terminal is less clear.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: Insulin negatively regulates FOXO via phosphorylation by Akt in both flies and rodents.
source: Insulin negatively regulates FOXO via phosphorylation by Akt in both flies and rodents (Puig et al., 2003; Teleman et al., 2005; Yamamoto and Tatar, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXO is required in Drosophila larval motor neurons for synapse growth, synaptic vesicle recycling, and for the control of neuronal excitability downstream of PI3K signaling.
source: Previous studies have established that FOXO is required in Drosophila larval motor neurons for synapse growth, synaptic vesicle recycling, and for the control of neuronal excitability downstream of PI3K signaling (Howlett et al., 2008; Nechipurenko and Broihier, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXO6 is required during learning and memory in mammals.
source: In mammals, recent studies have revealed a requirement for FOXO6, a FOXO family member highly expressed in the hippocampus, during learning and memory (Salih et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXO6 is required for the expression of genes involved in neurotransmission.
source: It was shown in these studies that FOXO6 was required for the expression of genes involved in neurotransmission supporting a direct role for FOXO in the regulation of synapse function (Salih et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It is unclear whether insulin signaling regulates FOXO activity in neurons in any system.
source: It is unclear whether insulin signaling regulates FOXO activity in neurons in any system.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: In adult Drosophila motor neurons, insulin signaling negatively regulates the presynaptic release of neurotransmitter via the FOXO-dependent regulation of the translational inhibitor the eukaryotic initiation factor 4e binding protein (4eBP).
source: In the present study, we present evidence that in adult Drosophila motor neurons, insulin signaling negatively regulates the presynaptic release of neurotransmitter via the FOXO-dependent regulation of the translational inhibitor the eukaryotic initiation factor 4e binding protein (4eBP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The translational target of the insulin-FOXO-4eBP signaling system appears to be the Complexin protein.
source: The translational target of this signaling system appears to be the Complexin protein, which is known to regulate the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles providing direct link between neuronal insulin signaling and neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Complexin mRNA binds to Staufen and Complexin levels are regulated by diet and insulin signaling.

claim: Complexin is known to regulate the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: The translational target of this signaling system appears to be the Complexin protein, which is known to regulate the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles providing direct link between neuronal insulin signaling and neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Complexin function.

claim: Animals raised for 21 days on food containing 100 mg/ml of yeast (1X) release nearly twice as much neurotransmitter compared to flies raised on food containing 200 mg/ml of yeast (2X).
source: Animals raised for 21 days on food containing 100 mg/ml of yeast (1X) release nearly twice as much neurotransmitter, represented as quantal content (the number of quanta per action potential) (Fatt and Katz, 1951), compared to flies raised on food containing 200 mg/ml of yeast (2X) (Figure 1B–F; see Table 1 for all electrophysiological recording data).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Shifting 20-day-old flies from the 1X diet to the 2X diet resulted in a gradual reduction in the quantal content that reaches the level of neurotransmission observed in 2X animals within 24 hr of diet shift.
source: We further find that shifting 20-day-old flies from the 1X diet to the 2X diet (Figure 1B) resulted in a gradual reduction in the quantal content (QC) that reaches the level of neurotransmission observed in 2X animals within 24 hr of diet shift (Figure 1C and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The effects of high-protein diet on release are likely not due to the accumulation of diet-related pathologies that result in reduced neurotransmitter release.
source: We further find that shifting 20-day-old flies from the 1X diet to the 2X diet (Figure 1B) resulted in a gradual reduction in the quantal content (QC) that reaches the level of neurotransmission observed in 2X animals within 24 hr of diet shift (Figure 1C and F) supporting that the effects of high-protein diet on release are likely not due to the accumulation of diet-related pathologies that result in reduced neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rapid reversibility of the diet effect within 24 hours.

claim: Diet has no effect on the amplitude of the spontaneous release events (mEPSPs), the resting membrane potential, or the resistance of the muscle.
source: In these recordings, we observed no effect of diet on the amplitude of the spontaneous release events (mEPSPs), the resting membrane potential, or the resistance of the muscle demonstrating that the effects of diet on presynaptic function are not due to changes in the excitability of the post-synaptic CM9 muscle fibers (Figure 1E; Table 1) (Davis, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: The effects of diet on presynaptic function are not due to changes in the excitability of the post-synaptic CM9 muscle fibers.
source: In these recordings, we observed no effect of diet on the amplitude of the spontaneous release events (mEPSPs), the resting membrane potential, or the resistance of the muscle demonstrating that the effects of diet on presynaptic function are not due to changes in the excitability of the post-synaptic CM9 muscle fibers (Figure 1E; Table 1) (Davis, 2013).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of changes in postsynaptic properties.

claim: Flies raised on 1X diet show pronounced synaptic depression when EPSPs were evoked with a 50-ms interpulse interval that was absent at CM9 NMJs in flies raised on the 2X diet.
source: Paired pulse analysis at the CM9 NMJ reveals that flies raised on 1X diet show pronounced synaptic depression when EPSPs were evoked with a 50-ms interpulse interval that was absent at CM9 NMJs in flies raised on the 2X diet (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The paired-pulse depression result is consistent with a reduction in the probability of release at CM9 NMJs in animals subjected to the 2X diet.
source: Under our recording conditions, this result is consistent with a reduction in the probability of release at CM9 NMJs in animals subjected to the 2X diet (Zucker and Regehr, 2002).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the paired-pulse data and supported by citation to established principles of synaptic physiology.

claim: There is no significant difference in the size of the sucrose-sensitive pool of synaptic vesicles (SVs) at the CM9 NMJs in flies raised on a 1X diet compared to flies raised on a 2X diet.
source: We find that there is no significant difference in the size of the sucrose-sensitive pool of synaptic vesicles (SVs) at the CM9 NMJs in flies raised on a 1X diet compared to flies raised on a 2X diet (Figure 1I–K) (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by hypertonic sucrose challenge data presented in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Increases in the protein content of the diet reduces the probability of SV release at the CM9 NMJ.
source: Combined with our previous observations of a lack of effect of diet on synaptic area (Rawson et al., 2012), these data support that increases in the protein content of the diet reduces the probability of SV release at the CM9 NMJ.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple lines of electrophysiological data including quantal content, paired-pulse, and readily-releasable pool measurements.

claim: Knockdown of 4eBP in the CM9 motor neuron reduced the presynaptic release of neurotransmitter in animals raised on a 1X diet compared to controls.
source: Analysis of neurotransmission in these animals found that knockdown of 4eBP in the CM9 motor neuron reduced the presynaptic release of neurotransmitter in animals raised on a 1X diet compared to controls (Figure 2F–I; see Table 1 for E49-Gal4/+ control values).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2F-I and Table 1.

claim: There is no difference between neurotransmitter release in 4eBP knockdown animals (4eBPRNAi) raised on 1X, 2X, or 1-2X diet conditions.
source: We also observe no difference between neurotransmitter release in 4eBP knockdown animals (4eBPRNAi) raised on 1X, 2X, or 1-2X diet conditions consistent with the effects of 4eBP knockdown being specific to diet regulation of neurotransmission and not basal release (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2F-I.

claim: The effects of 4eBP knockdown are specific to diet regulation of neurotransmission and not basal release.
source: We also observe no difference between neurotransmitter release in 4eBP knockdown animals (4eBPRNAi) raised on 1X, 2X, or 1-2X diet conditions consistent with the effects of 4eBP knockdown being specific to diet regulation of neurotransmission and not basal release (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that 4eBP knockdown eliminates diet-dependent differences in neurotransmission.

claim: Both the 2X diet and the 1-2X diet shift conditions resulted in increased phosphorylation of InR and Akt compared to the 1X diet condition.
source: This analysis found that both the 2X diet and the 1-2X diet shift conditions resulted in increased phosphorylation of InR and Akt compared to the 1X diet condition supporting that our 2X and 1-2X diet conditions result in increased insulin signaling in our flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data showing increased phosphorylation of insulin signaling components.

claim: The 2X and 1-2X diet conditions result in increased insulin signaling in flies.
source: This analysis found that both the 2X diet and the 1-2X diet shift conditions resulted in increased phosphorylation of InR and Akt compared to the 1X diet condition supporting that our 2X and 1-2X diet conditions result in increased insulin signaling in our flies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased phosphorylation of InR and Akt, which are markers of insulin signaling activity.

claim: CM9-specific knock-down of the Drosophila IRS-1 homologue chico (chicoRNAi) in flies raised on the 2X and 1-2X shift diets resulted in a significant increase SV release compared to the 2X controls.
source: Consistent with insulin signaling in the CM9 motor neuron being responsible for the effects of diet on SV release, we observe that CM9-specific knock-down of the Drosophila IRS-1 homologue chico (chicoRNAi) in flies raised on the 2X and 1-2X shift diets resulted in a significant increase SV release compared to the 2X controls (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2J-L.

claim: The effect of chico knockdown on SV release in flies raised on the 2X diet was phenocopied by the overexpression of a dominant negative insulin receptor (InRDN) in the CM9 motor neuron.
source: This effect of chicoRNAion SV release in flies raised on the 2X diet was phenocopied by the overexpression of a dominant negative insulin receptor (InRDN) in the CM9 motor neuron (Figure 2K and L) (Peru Y Colón de Portugal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2K and L.

claim: There is no difference in neurotransmitter release between chicoRNAi animals raised on 1X, 2X or 1-2X diets versus 1X controls, except that chicoRNAi animals raised on 1X have slightly increased EPSPs compared to 1X controls.
source: We also observe that there is no difference in neurotransmitter release between chicoRNAi animals raised on 1X, 2X or 1-2X diets versus 1X controls (Figure 2K and L), except that chicoRNAi animals raised on 1X have slightly increased EPSPs (p=0.032) compared to 1X controls consistent with low-level insulin signaling even in animals raised on a 1X diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2K and L.

claim: Low-level insulin signaling occurs even in animals raised on a 1X diet.
source: We also observe that there is no difference in neurotransmitter release between chicoRNAi animals raised on 1X, 2X or 1-2X diets versus 1X controls (Figure 2K and L), except that chicoRNAi animals raised on 1X have slightly increased EPSPs (p=0.032) compared to 1X controls consistent with low-level insulin signaling even in animals raised on a 1X diet.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that chico knockdown slightly increases EPSPs even in 1X diet animals.

claim: The increase in neurotransmitter release observed in the chicoRNAi flies raised on the 2X diet was suppressed by the simultaneous knock-down of 4eBP.
source: Finally, the increase in neurotransmitter release observed in the chicoRNAi flies raised on the 2X diet was suppressed by the simultaneous knock-down of 4eBP (Figure 2K–L), consistent with 4eBP functioning downstream of Chico during the regulation of neurotransmission in response to diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2K-L showing epistasis between chico and 4eBP.

claim: 4eBP functions downstream of Chico during the regulation of neurotransmission in response to diet.
source: Finally, the increase in neurotransmitter release observed in the chicoRNAi flies raised on the 2X diet was suppressed by the simultaneous knock-down of 4eBP (Figure 2K–L), consistent with 4eBP functioning downstream of Chico during the regulation of neurotransmission in response to diet.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the epistasis experiment showing that 4eBP knockdown suppresses the effect of chico knockdown.

claim: The epistasis between chico and 4eBP is similar to what has been recently observed for Drosophila lifespan.
source: This epistasis between chico and 4eBP is similar to what has been recently observed for Drosophila lifespan (Bai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The regulation of neurotransmission by insulin signaling appears to be specific to the adult life stage.
source: The regulation of neurotransmission by insulin signaling appears to be specific to the adult life stage since we do not observe the same effects of diet or presynaptic knockdown of 4eBP or chico on SV release from larval NMJs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from larval NMJs presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Insulin signaling results in the translation of a negative regulator(s) of SV release.
source: Because of the role of 4eBP in the inhibition of translation, our data suggests that insulin signaling results in the translation of a negative regulator(s) of SV release (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the role of 4eBP as a translational inhibitor and the effects of insulin signaling on neurotransmission.

claim: Cycloheximide effectively inhibits the reduction in SV release in response to a shift from 1X to 2X diet conditions.
source: We find that cycloheximide effectively inhibits the reduction in SV release in response to a shift from 1X to 2X diet conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and E) without significant effects on the amplitudes of the mEPSPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from cycloheximide-treated animals presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased insulin signaling results in the translation of a negative regulator(s) of SV release.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with increased insulin signaling resulting in the translation of a negative regulator(s) of SV release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cycloheximide experiment showing that blocking translation prevents the diet-induced reduction in neurotransmission.

claim: The activity of Drosophila 4eBP can be positively regulated transcriptionally by the Drosophila forkhead transcription factor dFOXO.
source: The activity of Drosophila 4eBP can be positively regulated transcriptionally by the Drosophila forkhead transcription factor dFOXO (Figure 3A) (Puig et al., 2003; Teleman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 4eBP mRNA levels in thoracic motor neurons are sensitive to diet.
source: Analysis of 4eBP mRNA levels in thoracic motor neurons purified by FACS from flies raised on a 1X diet, a 2X diet, or subjected to a diet switch from a 1X diet to a 2X diet reveals that 4eBP mRNA levels are sensitive to diet and that during diet shift the declines in 4eBP mRNA levels (Figure 3B) correlate with our observed declines in SV release (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from FACS-sorted motor neurons presented in Figure 3B.

claim: During diet shift the declines in 4eBP mRNA levels correlate with observed declines in SV release.
source: Analysis of 4eBP mRNA levels in thoracic motor neurons purified by FACS from flies raised on a 1X diet, a 2X diet, or subjected to a diet switch from a 1X diet to a 2X diet reveals that 4eBP mRNA levels are sensitive to diet and that during diet shift the declines in 4eBP mRNA levels (Figure 3B) correlate with our observed declines in SV release (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing qRT-PCR data (Figure 3B) with electrophysiological data (Figure 1F).

claim: The effects of diet on SV release are due to the transcriptional regulation of 4eBP.
source: This suggested that the effects of diet on SV release are due to the transcriptional regulation of 4eBP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between 4eBP mRNA levels and neurotransmission.

claim: dFOXO-binding sites exist near the 5' end of the 4eBP gene.
source: Previous studies have identified dFOXO-binding sites near the 5' end of the 4eBP gene (Puig et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: dFOXO-binding sites in the 4eBP promoter region were enriched in dFOXO ChIP of thoracic ganglion isolated from animals raised on a 1X diet as compared to animals raised on a 2X diet.
source: Using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) with anti-FOXO antibodies, we found that these dFOXO-binding sites in the 4eBP promoter region were enriched in our dFOXO ChIP of thoracic ganglion isolated from animals raised on a 1X diet as compared to animals raised on a 2X diet (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The difference in dFOXO binding to the 4eBP promoter was not due to changes in dFOXO protein levels under the diet conditions.
source: This difference was not due to changes in dFOXO protein levels under our diet conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: dFOXO binding to the 4eBP gene is increased under 1X diet condition compared to the 2X diet condition.
source: This supports that dFOXO binding to the 4eBP gene is increased under our 1X diet condition compared to the 2X diet condition consistent with dFOXO driving the expression of 4eBP under 1X diet conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIP data showing increased dFOXO binding to the 4eBP promoter in 1X diet conditions.

claim: dFOXO drives the expression of 4eBP under 1X diet conditions.
source: This supports that dFOXO binding to the 4eBP gene is increased under our 1X diet condition compared to the 2X diet condition consistent with dFOXO driving the expression of 4eBP under 1X diet conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIP data and the correlation with 4eBP mRNA levels.

claim: The regulation of 4eBP mRNA levels by diet is conserved among all motor neurons and not specific to CM9 MNs.
source: Importantly, these molecular data suggest that the regulation of 4eBP mRNA levels by diet is conserved among all motor neurons and not specific to CM9 MNs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that the molecular analyses were performed on thoracic motor neurons, not specifically CM9 motor neurons.

claim: Neurotransmission is reduced in dFOXO mutants compared to 1X controls but are not different than the 2X controls.
source: Electrophysiological recordings from CM9 NMJs in dFOXO mutants raised on 1X, 2X or 1-2X shift diets found that neurotransmission is reduced in dFOXO mutants compared to 1X controls but are not different than the 2X controls, similar to what we observed in the 4eBPRNAi flies (Figure 3E–G, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from dFOXO mutants presented in Figure 3E-G and Table 1.

claim: The deficit in neurotransmission at the CM9 NMJs in dFOXO mutants is reversed by the over-expression of 4eBP in the CM9 motor neuron.
source: Further, this deficit in neurotransmission at the CM9 NMJs is reversed by the over-expression of 4eBP in the CM9 motor neuron in dFOXO mutants (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from dFOXO mutants with 4eBP overexpression presented in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Overexpression of 4eBP (4eBP OE) increases neurotransmission compared to 1X controls.
source: We also observe that overexpression of 4eBP (4eBP OE) increases neurotransmission compared to 1X controls consistent with persistent insulin signaling in animals on the 1X diet (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from 4eBP overexpression animals presented in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Persistent insulin signaling occurs in animals on the 1X diet.
source: We also observe that overexpression of 4eBP (4eBP OE) increases neurotransmission compared to 1X controls consistent with persistent insulin signaling in animals on the 1X diet (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that 4eBP overexpression increases neurotransmission even in 1X diet animals.

claim: The negative regulation of neurotransmitter release by insulin signaling involves repression of the dFOXO-dependent gene transcription of the 4eBP locus.
source: These results support the model that the negative regulation of neurotransmitter release by insulin signaling involves repression of the dFOXO-dependent gene transcription of the 4eBP locus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined genetic, molecular, and electrophysiological data showing the relationship between insulin signaling, FOXO, 4eBP, and neurotransmission.

claim: The phosphorylation, and subsequent inhibition, of 4eBP by mTOR is an established mechanism for regulating protein translation in response to changes in diet.
source: The phosphorylation, and subsequent inhibition, of 4eBP by mTOR is an established mechanism for regulating protein translation in response to changes in diet (Figure 4A) (Gingras et al., 1999) (Ma and Blenis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Postsynaptic TOR signaling can influence synapse function.
source: Previous studies have established that postsynaptic TOR signaling can influence synapse function (Penney et al., 2012; Weston et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TOR signaling has been linked to a number of important neuronal processes including the regulation of synapse structure and function.
source: Furthermore, TOR signaling has been linked to a number of important neuronal processes including the regulation of synapse structure and function (Bidinosti et al., 2010; Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009; Kelleher et al., 2004; Stoica et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rapamycin treatment was sufficient to reduce the phosphorylation of S6 kinase (P-S6K) and 4eBP (P-4eBP) supporting successful inhibition of dTOR.
source: This treatment paradigm was sufficient to reduce the phosphorylation of S6 kinase (P-S6K) and 4eBP (P-4eBP) supporting successful inhibition of dTOR under these feeding paradigm (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data presented in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Rapamycin treatment had no effect on the reduction of neurotransmitter release observed in response to the 1X to 2X diet shift.
source: Despite the change in phosphorylation of 4eBP, we observed no effect of the rapamycin treatment on the reduction of neurotransmitter release observed in response to the 1X to 2X diet shift (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from rapamycin-treated animals presented in Figure 4E-G.

claim: The effects of insulin signaling on SV exocytosis are largely independent of dTOR signaling.
source: These data are consistent with the effects of insulin signaling on SV exocytosis being largely independent of dTOR signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that rapamycin does not prevent the diet-induced reduction in neurotransmission despite inhibiting TOR.

claim: Rapamycin treatment results in the predicted change in the phosphorylation state of 4eBP demonstrating that TOR can regulate 4eBP in adult Drosophila motor neurons.
source: Importantly, we observe that our rapamycin treatment condition does result in the predicted change in the phosphorylation state of 4eBP demonstrating that TOR can regulate 4eBP in adult Drosophila motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data showing changes in 4eBP phosphorylation with rapamycin treatment.

claim: The RNAi knockdown of Staufen (staufenRNAi) in CM9 motor neurons blocked the reduction in neurotransmitter in response to diet shift.
source: Similar to what we observed with cycloheximide, we found the RNAi knockdown of Staufen (staufenRNAi) in CM9 motor neurons blocked the reduction in neurotransmitter in response to diet shift (Figure 5A,C and D) without altering muscle sensitivity to glutamate (Figure 5B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from Staufen knockdown animals presented in Figure 5A, C, and D.

claim: Staufen knockdown does not alter muscle sensitivity to glutamate.
source: Similar to what we observed with cycloheximide, we found the RNAi knockdown of Staufen (staufenRNAi) in CM9 motor neurons blocked the reduction in neurotransmitter in response to diet shift (Figure 5A,C and D) without altering muscle sensitivity to glutamate (Figure 5B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSP data from Staufen knockdown animals presented in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claim: A Staufen bound mRNA is involved in the effects of diet on neurotransmitter release.
source: These results support the model that a Staufen bound mRNA is involved in the effects of diet on neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Staufen knockdown blocks the diet effect on neurotransmission.

claim: The collection of mRNAs bound to Staufen2 in mammalian brain tissues includes a number of important presynaptic regulators of synapse function.
source: Recently, the collection of mRNAs bound to Staufen2 in mammalian brain tissues was defined and a number of important presynaptic regulators of synapse function were identified (Heraud-Farlow et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Complexin mRNA was identified as bound to Staufen2 in mammalian brain tissues.
source: One of the mRNAs identified in this study was the mRNA encoding complexin, a small peptide that functions as both a facilitator and an inhibitor of SV exocytosis (Südhof, 2012; Trimbuch and Rosenmund, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Complexin is a small peptide that functions as both a facilitator and an inhibitor of SV exocytosis.
source: One of the mRNAs identified in this study was the mRNA encoding complexin, a small peptide that functions as both a facilitator and an inhibitor of SV exocytosis (Südhof, 2012; Trimbuch and Rosenmund, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Drosophila complexin mRNA contains predicted Staufen target sequences (STSs).
source: In addition, Drosophila complexin mRNA contains predicted Staufen target sequences (STSs) (Laver et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Complexin mRNA was highly enriched in Staufen RIPs from motor neurons.
source: These analyses revealed that complexin mRNA was highly enriched in Staufen RIPs from motor neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: 4eBP mRNA was highly enriched in Staufen RIPs from motor neurons even though 4eBP mRNAs do not contain a predicted STS.
source: Surprisingly, we also observed that 4eBP mRNA was also highly enriched even though 4eBP mRNAs do not contain a predicted STS (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: The RIP of complexin and 4eBP mRNA was specific since a number of other neuronal mRNAs were not enriched in these RIP experiments including mRNAs for tubulin, syntaxin and the cacophony voltage-gated calcium channel.
source: The RIP of complexin and 4eBP mRNA was specific since a number of other neuronal mRNAs were not enriched in these RIP experiments including mRNAs for tubulin, syntaxin and the cacophony voltage-gated calcium channel (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 5E showing negative controls.

claim: Complexin levels at the CM9 NMJ is increased in animals on a 2X diet compared to animals on the 1X diet.
source: Immunofluorescent microscopy of CM9 NMJs in flies raised on 1X and 2X diets found that Complexin staining was increased at CM9 NMJs in animals on a 2X diet compared to animals on the 1X diet (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The average maximum pixel intensity of Complexin staining is significantly increased at NMJs from animals raised on the 2X diet compared to the 1X diet.
source: We used deconvolution microscopy to quantify the intensity of Complexin staining at the CM9 NMJ and find that the average maximum pixel intensity of Complexin staining is significantly increased at NMJs from animals raised on the 2X diet compared to the 1X diet (Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The distribution of maximum pixel intensity values for Complexin is significantly different between 1X and 2X diet conditions.
source: We used deconvolution microscopy to quantify the intensity of Complexin staining at the CM9 NMJ and find that the average maximum pixel intensity of Complexin staining is significantly increased at NMJs from animals raised on the 2X diet compared to the 1X diet (Figure 6C) and that the distribution of m.p.i values is also significantly different (Figure 6D; see source data file for Kolmogorov-Smirmov test results).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: chicoRNAi animals raised on a 2X diet had significantly reduced Complexin levels.
source: Furthermore, chicoRNAi animals raised on a 2X diet had significantly reduced Complexin levels (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: There is significantly more Complexin at the LAM NMJs in flies raised on a 2X diet compared to flies raised on a 1X diet.
source: Using an identical approach to quantifying Complexin at the CM9 NMJs, we find that there is significantly more Complexin at the LAM NMJs in flies raised on a 2X diet compared to flies raised on a 1X diet supporting that this signaling system is present in LAM motor neurons as well (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data from LAM NMJs presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The insulin-FOXO-4eBP-Complexin signaling system is present in LAM motor neurons.
source: Using an identical approach to quantifying Complexin at the CM9 NMJs, we find that there is significantly more Complexin at the LAM NMJs in flies raised on a 2X diet compared to flies raised on a 1X diet supporting that this signaling system is present in LAM motor neurons as well (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Complexin levels at LAM NMJs are also diet-sensitive.

claim: Reduction of one copy of the complexin gene (cpxSH1/+) significantly increases quantal content at CM9 NMJs in animals raised on both the 1X and 2X diets compared to controls.
source: Functionally, we find that reduction of one copy of the complexin gene (cpxSH1/+) significantly increases quantal content at CM9 NMJs in animals raised on both the 1X and 2X diets compared to controls (Figure 6E and F, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from complexin heterozygotes presented in Figure 6E and F and Table 1.

claim: There is a significant increase in the frequency of spontaneous SV fusion events in cpxSH1/+ animals.
source: We also observe a significant increase in the frequency of spontaneous SV fusion events in cpxSH1/+ animals consistent with previous observations at the Drosophila larval NMJ (Figure 6H) (Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6H and citation to prior literature.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the amount of Complexin at the synapse in the cpxSH1/+ animals compared to wild type.
source: Fluorescent microscopic quantification of synaptic complexin levels reveals a significant reduction in the amount of Complexin at the synapse in the cpxSH1/+ animals compared to wild type (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6J.

claim: Overexpression of Complexin in the CM9 motor neuron of animals raised on a 1X diet reduces quantal content compared to 1X diet controls.
source: Conversely, we observe a reduction in quantal content if we overexpress Complexin in the CM9 motor neuron of animals raised on a 1X diet compared to 1X diet controls (Figure 6K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from Complexin overexpression animals presented in Figure 6K-M.

claim: Overexpression of Complexin in animals on 2X diets does not reduce neurotransmission further compared to 2X diet controls.
source: We also find that overexpression of Complexin in animals on 2X diets does not reduce neurotransmission further compared to 2X diet controls similar to our data with 4eBP, chico and dFOXO (Figure 6L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6L and M.

claim: Diet can influence neurotransmission at the adult NMJ by regulating the synaptic levels of Complexin.
source: These data are consistent with the model that diet can influence neurotransmission at the adult NMJ by regulating the synaptic levels of Complexin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing diet-dependent changes in Complexin levels and the effects of genetic manipulation of Complexin on neurotransmission.

claim: Insulin signaling in adult Drosophila motor neurons can negatively regulate the release of neurotransmitter from the NMJ.
source: Here, we have revealed that insulin signaling in adult Drosophila motor neurons can negatively regulate the release of neurotransmitter from the NMJ.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding supported by all the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The control of neurotransmission by insulin signaling utilizes the FOXO transcription factor to transcriptionally regulate the eukaryotic initiation factor 4e binding protein (4eBP).
source: This control of neurotransmission by insulin signaling utilizes the FOXO transcription factor to transcriptionally regulate the eukaryotic initiation factor 4e binding protein (4eBP, also known as Thor in Drosophila), a negative regulator of cap-dependent translation (Gingras et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding supported by genetic, molecular, and electrophysiological data.

claim: 4eBP is a negative regulator of cap-dependent translation.
source: This control of neurotransmission by insulin signaling utilizes the FOXO transcription factor to transcriptionally regulate the eukaryotic initiation factor 4e binding protein (4eBP, also known as Thor in Drosophila), a negative regulator of cap-dependent translation (Gingras et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The control of neurotransmitter release by insulin signaling is dependent on the diet conditions and likely does not reflect a role for insulin in basal neurotransmitter release.
source: Importantly, our data suggest that the control of neurotransmitter release by insulin signaling is dependent on the diet conditions and likely does not reflect a role for insulin in basal neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that genetic manipulations of insulin signaling components eliminate diet-dependent differences but do not necessarily alter basal neurotransmission.

claim: Repression of FOXO activity due to insulin signaling results in reduced levels of 4eBP mRNA, subsequent increased protein translation, and reduced SV release.
source: Our data supports the model that repression of FOXO activity due to insulin signaling results in reduced levels of 4eBP mRNA, subsequent increased protein translation, and reduced SV release.
evidence: This claim represents a model inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: The activity of 4eBP is regulated by phosphorylation via the actions of the target of rapamycin complex (TOR).
source: The activity of 4eBP is also regulated by phosphorylation via the actions of the target of rapamycin complex (TOR) (Beretta et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Numerous studies have implicated the TOR complex in the regulation of synapse function.
source: The activity of 4eBP is also regulated by phosphorylation via the actions of the target of rapamycin complex (TOR) (Beretta et al., 1996) and numerous studies have implicated the TOR complex in the regulation of synapse function (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009; Hoeffer and Klann, 2010; Penney et al., 2012; Takei et al., 2004; Weston et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The regulation of neurotransmission by diet at the CM9 NMJ appears to be largely independent of TOR.
source: The regulation of neurotransmission by diet at the CM9 NMJ appears to be largely independent of TOR since the effect of diet on neurotransmission is not affected by rapamycin, a potent inhibitor of the TOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rapamycin experiment showing no effect on diet-induced changes in neurotransmission.

claim: Rapamycin treatment results in the predicted change in the phosphorylation state of 4eBP demonstrating that TOR can regulate 4eBP in adult Drosophila motor neurons.
source: Importantly, we observe that our rapamycin treatment condition does result in the predicted change in the phosphorylation state of 4eBP demonstrating that TOR can regulate 4eBP in adult Drosophila motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data showing changes in 4eBP phosphorylation with rapamycin treatment.

claim: Most of the data on the effects of TOR on synapse function suggest a post-synaptic role for this complex.
source: Because most of the data on the effects of TOR on synapse function suggest a post-synaptic role for this complex, these data suggest that the regulation of 4eBP within the CM9 motor neuron is compartmentalized with the presynaptic pool regulated specifically by FOXO and the post-synaptic pool regulated by TOR.
evidence: This claim is based on review of existing literature.

claim: The regulation of 4eBP within the CM9 motor neuron is compartmentalized with the presynaptic pool regulated specifically by FOXO and the post-synaptic pool regulated by TOR.
source: Because most of the data on the effects of TOR on synapse function suggest a post-synaptic role for this complex, these data suggest that the regulation of 4eBP within the CM9 motor neuron is compartmentalized with the presynaptic pool regulated specifically by FOXO and the post-synaptic pool regulated by TOR.
evidence: This claim is a speculative model inferred from the data and existing literature.

claim: The localization of the TOR complex in neurons is unknown.
source: The localization of the TOR complex in neurons is unknown, but it presumably is localized within the cytoplasm and lysosomes (Betz and Hall, 2013).
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap with speculation based on citation.

claim: There exist three members of the 4eBP family in mammals with 4eBP2 being the most highly expressed family member in the brain.
source: There exist three members of the 4eBP family in mammals with 4eBP2 being the most highly expressed family member in the brain (Banko et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: 4eBP2 is required for a broad range of cognitive and motor behaviors in mice.
source: Analysis of 4eBP2 knock-out mice has revealed that this protein is required for a broad range of cognitive and motor behaviors (Banko et al., 2007; Gkogkas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The changes in behavior observed in 4eBP2 knock-out mice correlate with changes in synapse function that are highlighted by changes in post-synaptic glutamate receptor function.
source: The changes in behavior observed in 4eBP2 knock-out mice correlate with changes in synapse function that are highlighted by changes in post-synaptic glutamate receptor function (Banko et al., 2005; Bidinosti et al., 2010; Gkogkas et al., 2013; Ran et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is no evidence from studies of 4eBP2 knock-out mice of an effect on presynaptic function.
source: To date, there is no evidence from these studies of an effect of the 4eBP2 knock-out on presynaptic function.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on review of existing literature.

claim: 4eBP2 has been implicated in the regulation of neuroligin levels.
source: In addition to effects on glutamate receptor function, 4eBP2 has also been implicated in the regulation of neuroligin levels (Gkogkas et al., 2013; Khoutorsky et al., 2015), a post-synaptic scaffolding protein that functions to regulate synaptogenesis and neurotransmission (Craig and Kang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neuroligin is a post-synaptic scaffolding protein that functions to regulate synaptogenesis and neurotransmission.
source: In addition to effects on glutamate receptor function, 4eBP2 has also been implicated in the regulation of neuroligin levels (Gkogkas et al., 2013; Khoutorsky et al., 2015), a post-synaptic scaffolding protein that functions to regulate synaptogenesis and neurotransmission (Craig and Kang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The regulation of neurotransmission by neuroligin is likely due to its trans-synaptic interaction with the presynaptic binding protein neurexin.
source: The regulation of neurotransmission by neuroligin is likely due to its trans-synaptic interaction with the presynaptic binding protein neurexin, a cell adhesion molecule known to regulate synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Südhof, 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from established knowledge about neuroligin-neurexin interactions and supported by citation.

claim: Neurexin is a cell adhesion molecule known to regulate synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
source: The regulation of neurotransmission by neuroligin is likely due to its trans-synaptic interaction with the presynaptic binding protein neurexin, a cell adhesion molecule known to regulate synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Südhof, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Changes in post-synaptic neuroligin levels can result in increased presynaptic function, although this would represent a non-autonomous role for 4eBP on neurotransmitter release.
source: Thus, changes in post-synaptic neuroligin levels can result in increased presynaptic function, although this would represent a non-autonomous role for 4eBP on neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the trans-synaptic signaling mechanism of neuroligin-neurexin.

claim: It is unclear if altered neuroligin-neurexin signaling contributes to the neurotransmission phenotypes observed in the 4eBP2 knock-out mice.
source: It is unclear if altered neuroligin-neurexin signaling contributes to the neurotransmission phenotypes observed in the 4eBP2 knock-out mice.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: Phosphorylation of 4eBP by dTOR has no effect on the regulation of neurotransmitter release by insulin signaling in the CM9 MN.
source: We find that phosphorylation of 4eBP by dTOR has no effect on the regulation of neurotransmitter release by insulin signaling in the CM9 MN.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rapamycin experiment data.

claim: There might exist separate pools of 4eBP within the neuron that specify the effects of TOR versus FOXO on synapse function.
source: This result suggests that there might exist separate pools of 4eBP within the neuron that specify the effects of TOR versus FOXO on synapse function.
evidence: This claim is a speculative model inferred from the data.

claim: It is unclear how the compartmentalization of 4eBP activity is achieved within the pre- versus postsynaptic compartments.
source: Currently, it is unclear how the compartmentalization of 4eBP activity is achieved within the pre- versus postsynaptic compartments.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: Staufen binds to 4eBP mRNA in motor neurons.
source: We have found that Staufen binds to 4eBP mRNA in motor neurons and is required for the effects of diet on neurotransmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Staufen is required for the effects of diet on neurotransmission.
source: We have found that Staufen binds to 4eBP mRNA in motor neurons and is required for the effects of diet on neurotransmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from Staufen knockdown animals.

claim: Staufen is known to bind nascent mRNAs and mediate their nuclear export.
source: In addition to mRNA transport, Staufen is also known to bind nascent mRNAs and mediate their nuclear export (Elvira et al., 2006; Jansen and Niessing, 2012; Liu et al., 2006; Macchi et al., 2004; Miki and Yoneda, 2004; Miki et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The association of Staufen with nascent 4eBP mRNAs driven by FOXO might differentiate the dendritic from axonal populations of 4eBP.
source: Perhaps, the association of Staufen with nascent 4eBP mRNAs driven by FOXO differentiates the dendritic from axonal populations of 4eBP.
evidence: This claim is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Drosophila Staufen binds strongly to complexin mRNA.
source: In addition to 4eBP mRNA, we also find that Drosophila Staufen binds strongly to complexin mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Diet might control neurotransmission via the regulation of Complexin.
source: This suggested that diet might control neurotransmission via the regulation of Complexin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Staufen binds complexin mRNA and is required for diet effects on neurotransmission.

claim: The increased levels of Complexin in animals raised on the 2X diet inhibit the SV release.
source: In support of this model, we find that Complexin levels at the CM9 NMJ is increased in animals raised on a 2X diet compared to a 1X diet and that these levels are sensitive to changes in insulin signaling. This suggests that the increased levels of Complexin in animals raised on the 2X diet inhibit the SV release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between increased Complexin levels and reduced neurotransmission in 2X diet animals.

claim: Genetically altering complexin levels can influence neurotransmitter release from the CM9 NMJ in a diet-dependent manner similar to what is observed with 4eBP, chico and dFOXO mutants.
source: We also find that genetically altering complexin levels can influence neurotransmitter release from the CM9 NMJ in a diet-dependent manner similar to what is observed with 4eBP, chico and dFOXO mutants supporting the model that Complexin is an important target for the regulation of neuronal function by insulin signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from complexin genetic manipulations.

claim: Complexin is an important target for the regulation of neuronal function by insulin signaling.
source: We also find that genetically altering complexin levels can influence neurotransmitter release from the CM9 NMJ in a diet-dependent manner similar to what is observed with 4eBP, chico and dFOXO mutants supporting the model that Complexin is an important target for the regulation of neuronal function by insulin signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing Complexin is regulated by insulin signaling and affects neurotransmission.

claim: Both complexin and 4eBP mRNAs are bound to Staufen, so perhaps diet controls neurotransmitter release by altering the relative amounts of bound 4eBP to complexin mRNAs.
source: Because both complexin and 4eBP mRNAs are bound to Staufen, perhaps diet controls neurotransmitter release by altering the relative amounts of bound 4eBP to complexin mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: An acute increase in Complexin levels can inhibit neurotransmitter release at the CM9 NMJ.
source: The effects of our diet switch on neurotransmission support that an acute increase in Complexin levels can inhibit neurotransmitter release at the CM9 NMJ.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the diet shift experiment showing rapid changes in neurotransmission.

claim: Complexin is required for normal calcium-dependent SV exocytosis based on knock-out studies in mice, worms and Drosophila larvae.
source: It is clear from knock-out studies in mice, worms and Drosophila larvae that Complexin is required for normal calcium-dependent SV exocytosis and supports a facilitatory, not inhibitory, role for Complexin during neurotransmission (Cho et al., 2010; Jorquera et al., 2012; Radoff et al., 2014; Reim et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Knock-out studies support a facilitatory, not inhibitory, role for Complexin during neurotransmission.
source: It is clear from knock-out studies in mice, worms and Drosophila larvae that Complexin is required for normal calcium-dependent SV exocytosis and supports a facilitatory, not inhibitory, role for Complexin during neurotransmission (Cho et al., 2010; Jorquera et al., 2012; Radoff et al., 2014; Reim et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Other studies, including acute injections and vesicle targeting studies, have indicated that Complexin can also have an inhibitory role on evoked release.
source: But other studies, including acute injections and vesicle targeting studies, have indicated that Complexin can also have an inhibitory role on evoked release (Archer et al., 2002; Giraudo et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2007; Ono et al., 1998; Tang et al., 2006; Tokumaru et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Comparison of complexin knock-down to knock-out in different neuronal cell types suggest that the effects of Complexin on SV exocytosis can be sensitive to chronic versus acute manipulations and dependent upon neuronal cell type.
source: Further, comparison of complexin knock-down to knock-out in different neuronal cell types suggest that the effects of Complexin on SV exocytosis can be sensitive to chronic versus acute manipulations and dependent upon neuronal cell type (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Diet has no effect on SV release from Drosophila larval NMJs.
source: Although we find that diet has no effect on SV release from Drosophila larval NMJs, further studies will be needed to determine if this is due to differences between adult and larval motor neurons or to differences in the manipulations of Complexin.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from larval NMJs.

claim: It is likely that the effects of Complexin observed in this study require the co-translation of other exocytotic components.
source: In addition, it is likely that the effects of Complexin that we observe require the co-translation of other exocytotic components.
evidence: This claim is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: Increases in synaptic Complexin levels resulting from insulin signaling can reduce neurotransmitter release.
source: Regardless our data support the model that increases in synaptic Complexin levels resulting from insulin signaling can reduce neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim summarizes the model supported by the experimental data.

claim: The findings have broad implications for the effects of insulin signaling on the nervous system.
source: These results have broad implications for the effects of insulin signaling on the nervous system.
evidence: This claim is a general statement about the significance of the findings.
